deep.reconstruction:
OVERVIEW. The page compares an ephemeris computed from one set of elliptic elements of Ceres with Milan observations (Oriani) of 1805 Dec 29 (two observations), Dec 31, and 1806 Jan 5, 7 and 12. Ceres was then near opposition: RA about 103-106 deg, Sun longitude about 278-292 deg. The elements are the ones on the previous page: node about 80 deg 59', i about 10 deg 37', mean anomaly at epoch 322 deg 35'52.43'' (epoch Dec 31.0 = Jan 0.0 Paris mean time), log n = 2.8863074 (n about 769.67''/day), log e'' = 4.2216648 (e about 0.08075). The previous page did Jan 3 and Jan 4, and the next page collects all the residuals into 'ERRORES' and an 'Error normalis'. 'Litt. O' is apparently a label for this element system or set of comparisons; its precise meaning is unsure. Each date gets the same computation, in seven steps.

(1) TIME REDUCTION. Take the observed clock time t_obs. Subtract a small reduction of about 13 min, which varies slightly from entry to entry (13'7.82'', 13'8.16'', 13'11.44'', 13'9.56'', 13'11.42'', 13'10.97''); its nature is not certain. This gives Milan mean time.
- Add 6m11s (Milan to Seeberg/Gotha) to get Seeberg time.
- Subtract 33m35s (Seeberg to Paris) to get Paris time, expressed as a decimal fraction of the day.
- Jan 5: 11h58m0s - 13m7.82s = 11h44m52s Milan; + 6m11s = 11h51m3s Seeberg; Paris 11h17m28s = 11.29111 h, i.e. t = Jan 5.470463.
- Jan 7: 11h48m3s gives Paris Jan 7.463553.
- Jan 12: 11h31m52s gives Paris Jan 12.452275.
- Dec 31: 6h44m13s gives Paris Dec 31.252546.
- Dec 29: 9h37m42s and 13h15m36s give Paris Dec 29.372998 and 29.524317.

(2) MEAN ANOMALY. M = M0 + n*(t - t0).
- Jan 5: log 5.470463 = 0.7380241; adding 2.8863074 gives 4210.48'' = 1 deg 10'10.48''; M = 323 deg 46'2.91''.
- Jan 7: 5744.51'', M = 324 deg 11'36.94''.
- Jan 12: 9584.20'', M = 325 deg 15'36.63''.
- Dec 31: 194.38'' (3'14.38''), M = 322 deg 39'6.81''. An abandoned first attempt, 575.30'', corresponds to the wrong interval 1 - 0.252546 days.
- Dec 29: intervals backwards. log 1.627002 = 0.2113881 and log 1.475683 = 0.1689937 give 1252.26'' and 1135.80''; M = 322 deg 15'0.17'' and 322 deg 16'56.63''.

(3) KEPLER'S EQUATION. Solve M = E - e'' sin E with log e'' = 4.2216648.
- Jan 5: e'' sin E = -2 deg 55'19.10'' [log sin E = 9.8003140n], so E = 320 deg 50'43.81''.
- Jan 7: -2 deg 53'36.25'', E = 321 deg 18'0.69''.
- Jan 12: -2 deg 49'15.76'', E = 322 deg 26'20.87''.
- Dec 31: -2 deg 59'45.0'', E = 319 deg 39'21.89''.
- Dec 29: -3 deg 1'19.58'' and -3 deg 1'18.99'', E = 319 deg 13'40.59'' and 319 deg 15'44.64''.

(4) HELIOCENTRIC EQUATORIAL COORDINATES directly as functions of E (the form of Theoria Motus art. 56). For each axis k = x, y, z:
  k = a_k sin(A_k + E) + c_k.
- Amplitudes: log a_k = 0.4346953, 0.3997142, 0.1008078.
- Phases (previous page): A_x = 235 deg 57'8.85'', A_y = 150 deg 40'20.33'', A_z = 124 deg 34'32.69''.
- Constants c = (+0.1820815, -0.0993061, -0.0838776), the terms in -ae.
- Jan 5: A+E = 196 deg 47'52.66'', 111 deg 31'4.14'', 85 deg 25'16.50''. Log sines 9.4608944n, 9.9686247, 9.9986117 give a sin(A+E) = -0.7863025, +2.3352796, +1.2572438.

(5) SUN. Use von Zach's solar tables (Seeberg meridian).
- Mean longitude 9s 9 deg 25'47.31'' plus motion for days (5 d: 4 deg 55'41.65'') and Seeberg hours (29'12.11''), with the table arguments 4995.59, 348, 878, 542, 230.
- Add the equation of center (+10'48.83'', -0.10'') and the perturbations (-1.59, +3.31, +4.12). Add a nearly constant correction +37.86'' (identity unsure). Jan 5: L = 285 deg 2'13.50''.
- Radius vector as a number: 0.9832818 + 27 - 359 - 48 - 215 (units 1e-7) = 0.9832223.
- Then X = R cos L, Y = R cos eps sin L, Z = R sin eps sin L, using log R cos eps = 9.9551641 and log R sin eps = 9.5927439. Jan 5: X = +0.2550913, Y = -0.8710286, Z = -0.3781048.

(6) DIURNAL PARALLAX for Milan. Use local sidereal time theta (Jan 5: 101 deg 4'; Jan 7: 100 deg 47'20''; Dec 29: 58 deg 59' and 115 deg 10'; Jan 12: 101 deg 24').
- log(rho' cos phi * sin pi_sun) = 2.46626 in units of 1e-7.
- Corrections: -292.6 cos theta, -292.6 sin theta, and -297 in z. Jan 5: +56, -287, -297.
- So the computed vector is topocentric: planet heliocentric + Sun geocentric - observer.

(7) GEOCENTRIC PLACE.
- Jan 5: x = -0.3491241, y = 1.3649162, z = 0.7952317.
- tan alpha = y/x, giving alpha = 104 deg 20'51.84''.
- rho cos delta = y / sin alpha [log 0.1488675].
- tan delta = z / (rho cos delta), giving delta = 29 deg 26'33.35''.
- log rho = 0.2089248.
- 2.6875 is a constant written under each column, perhaps a light-time constant (log of about 487 s); unsure.
- Residuals: -34.16'' in RA and -15.55'' in Dec.

RESULTS for the other dates (computed place, then residuals in RA and Dec):
- Jan 7: 103 deg 49'34.61'', 29 deg 36'51.76''; -31.29'', -15.84''.
- Jan 12: 102 deg 32'14.34'' (or 20.01''), 30 deg 0'41.04''; -42.66'' 'as given', or -36.99'' with a meridian reduction; Dec -13.66'' / -15.34''.
- Dec 31: 105 deg 42'22.06'', 28 deg 57'40.66''; -41.64'', -20.24''.
- Dec 29: carried to the next page; -23.62'' / -13.76'' and -39.15'' / -13.62''.
- The next page averages the residuals to a normal error of about -35.5'' in RA and -15.2'' in Dec.

PURPOSE: a routine but meticulous test of a Ceres orbit against the 1805/06 opposition observations, to form normal places for orbit improvement.
errors: Dec 29 (first obs): 319 deg 13'40.59'' + 150 deg 40'20.33'' = 109 deg 54'0.92'', while the page (as transcribed) has 0.98''. This is either a misreading or a 0.06'' slip.

Dec 29 Sun: 279 deg 25'47.31'' - 1 deg 34'50.58'' = 277 deg 50'56.73'', not 56.93''. The next line, 277 deg 47'22.20'', is also about 0.03'' off from 56.93 - 3'34.76''. These are sub-arcsecond inconsistencies.
Dec 31: 322 deg 39'6.81'' - 2 deg 59'45.02'' = 319 deg 39'21.79'', while 21.89'' is written. The difference is 0.1'', perhaps from an extra iteration.
Dec 31: the first interval (575.30'', i.e. 0.747 days) was wrong. Gauss replaced it with 3'14.38'' (0.2525 days) and struck out part of the work.
Dec 29 second radius vector (0.9831759): the listed corrections (+151?, +27, -113, -306) do not visibly reproduce it from 0.9832166. Probably the base value was different; unresolved.
No substantive methodological errors; all checked logarithmic and coordinate sums agree to the 7th decimal.

results.what: Heliocentric equatorial coordinates of Ceres written as a sin(A+E) + c in the eccentric anomaly, with constants for the elements of 'Litt. O'
results.modern_name: Gaussian vectorial constants / ephemeris from orbital elements (Theoria Motus art. 56)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Theoria Motus 1809); equivalent forms in Lagrange/Laplace

results.what: Solution of Kepler's equation and topocentric RA/Dec including Sun's coordinates from von Zach's tables and diurnal parallax
Residuals of Milan observations of Ceres, Dec 29 1805 - Jan 12 1806, against the orbit, later averaged into a normal error

deep.surprise_reason: This is pure numerical ephemeris checking of Ceres against Oriani's 1805/06 opposition observations, exactly the documented routine of Gauss's orbit-improvement work. Nothing methodologically new appears.

checkable.asserts: equals 0.7380241 (log of the interval in days, Jan 5)
about 4210.48 arcsec = 1 deg 10'10.48'' (mean motion since epoch)
about 0: E = 320 deg 50'43.81'' solves Kepler's equation for M = 323 deg 46'2.91''
about 1.2572438 (so the transcribed 1.1572438 is a misreading)
about 4.03282, i.e. 10785'' = 2 deg 59'45'' (so log sin is 9.8111556 and the equation is 2 deg 59'45.02'', not 3 deg 59')
